sessions.title: Active Learning and Critical Thinking
sessions.content:
What does Active Learning look like?

Teachers:

  • Encourage students to ask and answer questions
  • Allow students to share and explore ideas
  • Guide students to connect learning to their own experiences, prior learning, and the real world
  • Challenge students to use higher order thinking skills
  • Encourage students to seek information and figure out problems on their own
  • Teach students specific active learning strategies
  • Avoid lectures and telling students what to do

Students:

  • Are engaged in activities (reading, thinking, writing, doing projects)
  • Ask and answer questions
  • Connect learning to their own experiences, prior learning, and the real world
  • Explore their own attitudes and values
  • Use higher order thinking skills (analysis, synthesis, evaluation)
  • Know how to find information
  • Solve problems
  • Use feedback from teachers and other students to complete learning and improve performance.

sessions.title: Critical Thinking in Detail
sessions.content:
Critical Thinking in Detail

Critical thinking is the intellectually disciplined process of actively and skillfully conceptualizing, applying, analyzing, synthesizing, and/or evaluating information gathered from, or generated by, observation, experience, reflection, reasoning, or communication.

Key Components (Higher Order Thinking):

  • Analyzing: Breaking information into parts to explore understandings and relationships (comparing, contrasting, categorizing).
  • Evaluating: Justifying a decision or course of action based on specific criteria and standards (checking, critiquing, judging).
  • Synthesizing/Creating: Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern (designing, constructing, planning, producing).

Question Stems to Encourage Critical Thinking:

  • What evidence supports your claim?
  • How would you solve this problem differently?
  • What are the potential biases in this information?
  • How is this connected to what we learned previously?
  • What would happen if...?

The Critical Thinking Process:

  1. Identify the issue: What is the real problem or question?
  2. Gather information: Seek relevant facts and evidence.
  3. Evaluate evidence: Determine the reliability and validity of the sources.
  4. Consider viewpoints: Analyze different perspectives.
  5. Draw conclusions: Make a reasoned judgment based on the evidence.
  6. Communicate findings: Explain the reasoning clearly.

sessions.title: Active Learning Strategies
sessions.content:
Active Learning Strategies

Conscience Alley: An activity in which one child takes on the role of a character while the other children create each side of an alley, putting forth their opposing views on the character's dilemma as the child in role walks between them. The character listens to his or her 'conscience' before making a decision about the course of action to take.

Hot-Seating: A drama activity in which a child takes on the role of a character in the 'hot seat', while the other children ask the character prepared or improvised questions.

Rainbow: An idea-sharing technique: discussion is paused and group members are given colours. They form new groups of children with the same colour and share their ideas.

Snowballing: An activity in which pairs discuss a subject and then join with another pair to form a group and share ideas. Two groups then join together and so on, until there is a whole-class discussion.

Thought Tracking: An activity in which the action in a story (such as a Role Play) is frozen at a key moment and the thoughts of a character are spoken aloud, either by a child in role or by a group.

Walking Bus: An activity in which music is played while the children walk around the classroom. When the music stops, the teacher asks a question that the children discuss with those nearest to them.

sessions.title: What is Formative Assessment?
indicators: How will the learner get to where they are going?
sessions.content:
What is Formative Assessment?

Formative assessment checks what students know during the learning process to see how their understanding and achievement can be improved.

Formative assessment (or assessment for learning) asks three key questions:

  1. Where is the learner going?
    • Set and clearly communicate the learning targets and success criteria.
    • Ensure teachers and students have a shared understanding of the learning goal.
    • Clear success criteria allow the teacher, learner, or peers to assess the work.
  2. Where is the learner now?
    • Gather evidence of what the students currently know and can do.
    • Use questioning, observations, discussions, and ongoing work to assess learning.
    • Use the evidence to adjust teaching and improve student understanding.
  3. How will the learner get to where they are going?
    • Use assessment information to identify what adjustments are needed.
    • Teachers adjust teaching activities, while students adjust learning behaviours and actions.
    • Formative assessment helps close the gap between current learning and desired outcomes.

sessions.title: Formative Assessment Strategies
sessions.content:
Formative Assessment Strategies

1. KWL Chart

What do you Know?What do you Want to know?What did you Learn?

KWL -> Learning Reflection Strategy (Identify learning needs)

  • K: What do I already know?
  • W: What do I Want to learn?
  • L: What have I Learned?

Example:
If a student has an upcoming science exam:

  • K: I know the basic parts of a cell.
  • W: I want to understand how cells reproduce.
  • L: I learned the stages of cell division.

2. Mind Map

Students create a visual representation of concepts (e.g., starting with the central concept of 'Water' and branching out to evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection, etc.).

Science vocabulary reference: https://sciencenotes.org/2013/12/science-solutions-vocabulary.html

3. Green Card/Red Card

Give green and red cards to each student in the class. Teacher stops presentation at various points to ask students to show either card before moving on with new material. Green card indicates they understand, red indicates they would like further input.

4. Pair Work

Teacher instructs pairs of students to go over the material they just learned, (before moving on in the presentation).

5. Exit Slips/Tickets

Students write out on an index card to questions about material in the presentation. Each student hands the cards in on the way out the door before leaving the class. Used to assess understanding (not for grading purposes).

6. 3-2-1

Upon leaving the classroom, students write down: 3 things they learned, 2 things they are interested in, and 1 thing they have a question about.

3 things you learned2 things that interest you1 question you have
1.1.1.
2.2.
3.

7. Peer-generated assessments

Ask students to write their own questions based on the lesson and ask each other these questions.

8. Concept sentences activity

Ask the students to create sentences using a set of key vocabulary words from the lesson. While they are writing, check their work - challenge any that are not correct by asking the pupil to explain them. Have some students read out sentences they have invented to whole class.

sessions.title: Summative Assessment
sessions.content:
Summative Assessment

Summative assessment checks what students have learned at the end of a learning period to determine their level of understanding, achievement, and attainment of the intended learning outcomes.

Summative assessment (or assessment of learning) asks three key questions:

  1. What has the learner achieved?
  2. How well has the learner achieved the expected outcomes?
  3. What should happen next?

Summative assessment provides a judgement of achievement and helps inform decisions about progression, certification, placement, or future learning.

Marking Guidance:

  • Apply the mark scheme carefully
  • Mark according to the objective the question is assessing
  • Moderate your marking with colleagues in your department
  • Think carefully about the message the assessment mark is giving parents
  • Give specific feedback about what a pupil needs to do to improve in the next test
  • Provide opportunities for them to work on areas which need improvement between tests
  • Use test data in collaboration with your teacher judgement

sessions.title: Opening Reflection
sessions.content:
Opening Reflection

Think about a pupil whose behaviour you find difficult to understand.

  • What do you notice first?
  • What assumptions might you make?
  • What happens immediately before the behaviour?
  • What does the child gain, avoid or communicate through the behaviour?

sessions.title: Challenging vs Disruptive Behaviour
sessions.content:
Challenging vs Disruptive Behaviour

The terms overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

Challenging - behaviour that is persistent, intense and/or significantly affects learning, relationships, participation or safety.

Challenging examples: repeated aggression, severe outbursts, persistent absconding or significant destruction.

Disruptive - behaviour that interferes with teaching, learning or classroom routines.

Disruptive examples: calling out, leaving seat, talking over others and distracting peers.

sessions.title: Understanding Stress
sessions.content:
Stress

Stress is the body's reaction to pressure or demands. It's what happens when you feel challenged, worried, or overwhelmed by a situation.

'Stress is how your body and mind feel when something is too hard or worrying.'

Not All Stress Is Harmful

  • POSITIVE - brief, manageable activation that can support adaptation and mastery.
  • TOLERABLE - more serious activation buffered by supportive relationships and recovery.
  • TOXIC - strong, frequent or prolonged activation without adequate buffering support.

sessions.title: How Stress Can Show Up in the Classroom
sessions.content:
How Stress Can Show Up in the Classroom

The same underlying stress can look different from child to child.

  • Hyperarousal: impulsivity, irritability, aggression, excessive movement or rapid reactions.
  • Withdrawal: silence, avoidance, head down, disengagement or seeming 'not to care'.
  • Attention difficulties: trouble holding instructions, starting work or shifting tasks.
  • Threat sensitivity: strong reactions to correction, peer conflict, noise or unexpected change.

When overwhelmed, reasoning and problem-solving may become harder.

Positive Stress: Challenge + Support

  • Examples: presenting, trying a difficult task, entering a new setting, competition or assessment.
  • Maintain high expectations while providing scaffolding and reassurance.
  • Teach coping skills rather than removing every uncomfortable challenge.
  • Goal: help the child experience 'I can handle this.'

Toxic Stress: When the Stress System Stays Activated

  • Teachers do not diagnose toxic stress.
  • Toxic stress involves excessive or prolonged activation of stress-response systems, particularly without adequate buffering support.
  • Possible classroom presentations include hypervigilance, aggression, impulsivity, shutdown, avoidance and difficulty concentrating.

sessions.title: Survival Responses in the Classroom
sessions.content:
Survival Responses in the Classroom

When children perceive threat or are overwhelmed, behaviour can shift toward protection.

  • FIGHT – confront, argue, shout, hit, push, challenge.
  • FLIGHT – escape, avoid, run, hide, wander, refuse.
  • FREEZE – shut down, stare, go quiet, become unable to start.
  • FAWN – over-please, apologise excessively, agree, fear disappointing.

sessions.title: Regulation Strategies
sessions.content:
Co-regulation Strategies

Co-regulation means that an adult (teacher, parent, caregiver) provides external support to help a child manage their emotions and behaviour until the child can self-regulate independently. It's about 'lending your calm' so the learner can regain control.

  • Two-metre rule: Keeping a safe physical distance when a child is dysregulated. This reduces perceived threat and gives the learner space to calm down while still feeling supported.
  • Low and Slow: Speaking in a calm, quiet, and slower tone of voice. This helps de-escalate heightened emotions and models self-control.
  • Reduced Demand: temporarily lowering expectations (e.g., fewer instructions, simpler tasks) so the child can focus on calming down rather than feeling overwhelmed.

Regulation Strategies

Regulating stress in different situations.

Two types of regulation strategies, Namely:

  • Co-regulation strategy
  • Self-regulation strategy

sessions.title: Self-Regulation Strategies
sessions.content:
Self-Regulation

Self-regulation is the ability of an individual to manage their own emotions, thoughts, and behaviours in order to stay calm, focused, and effective, especially in challenging situations. In education, it means learners can control impulses, handle stress, and make constructive choices without needing constant adult intervention.

Strategies for Self-Regulation:

  • Grounding Strategy: Techniques that bring attention back to the present moment (e.g., noticing five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear). Helps reduce anxiety and overwhelm.
  • Box breathing: A structured breathing exercise: inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4. This calms the nervous system and restores focus.
  • The wall push: A physical regulation technique where a learner pushes against a wall with their hands. It releases tension and provides sensory feedback to calm the body.

sessions.title: Additional Co-regulation and Communication Strategies
sessions.content:
Additional Regulation and Communication Strategies

  • Validating Mirroring: Acknowledging and reflecting the child's feelings ('I can see you're upset') without judgment. This shows empathy and helps the learner feel understood.
  • Rhythmic breathing together: Guiding the child to breathe slowly and steadily (e.g., 'In for 4, out for 4'). This regulates the nervous system and reduces stress.
  • Parallel Communication: Talking side-by-side rather than face-to-face. This reduces pressure and confrontation, making it easier for the child to listen and respond.
  • The safe exit (regulated pass): Allowing the child to leave the stressful situation safely (e.g., a quiet corner or designated calm space) to regain composure before rejoining the class.

sessions.title: Sensory and Movement Regulation
sessions.content:
Sensory and Movement Regulation Strategies

  • Brain breaks: Short, intentional pauses during learning (stretches, quick games, movement). They reset attention, reduce stress, and improve focus.
  • Sensory toolbox: A collection of calming items (stress balls, textured objects, calming scents, headphones). Learners use these to regulate emotions through sensory input.
  • Temperature shift: Using changes in temperature (cold water on hands, holding an ice cube, warm tea) to reset the body's stress response and bring calm.

sessions.title: Labeling and its Impact
sessions.content:
Labeling

Labeling in education refers to assigning a fixed description or category to a student based on their behaviour, ability, or background (e.g., 'lazy', 'slow learner', 'troublemaker', 'gifted').

It is essentially attaching an identity to a child that can shape how teachers, peers, and even the student themselves perceive their abilities and potential.

The impact of labeling student

  • Labels block progress.
  • They cause fixed mindsets leading to lowered expectations.
  • They confirm bias trap.
  • They damage self-efficacy.
  • They result in treating symptoms and ignoring the causes.
  • They cause low self-esteem.

sessions.title: Change the Lens: Describe, Don't Label
sessions.content:
Change the Lens: Describe, Don't Label

Language changes the questions we ask.

  • Instead of 'Larbi is naughty', describe what happened: 'Larbi pushed the chair away and shouted.'
  • Instead of 'He is lazy', ask: 'What happens when independent writing begins?'
  • Instead of 'She is attention-seeking', ask: 'What does she appear to gain from this interaction?'

Precise observation helps teachers identify triggers, functions and teachable skills.

Key principle: describe behaviour precisely rather than labelling the child.

sessions.title: The Teacher's Role in Improving Behaviour
sessions.content:
The Teacher's Role in Improving Behaviour

Teachers cannot control every behaviour, but they strongly influence the conditions around behaviour.

  • Build warm, predictable relationships.
  • Teach routines, expectations and replacement behaviours explicitly.
  • Design instruction that is appropriately challenging and accessible.
  • Notice patterns instead of reacting only to isolated incidents.
  • Use calm, consistent boundaries and logical consequences.
  • Collaborate with families and school support teams when concerns persist.
  • Use safeguarding procedures whenever there is a concern about safety or possible harm.

sessions.title: From Behaviour Management to Behaviour Teaching
sessions.content:
From Behaviour Management to Behaviour Teaching

The goal is not simply to suppress behaviour.

TRIGGER → STRESS/EMOTION → BEHAVIOUR → CONSEQUENCE → LEARNING

  • Identify the context and trigger.
  • Support regulation and safety.
  • Teach the missing skill or replacement behaviour.
  • Reinforce success and repair when things go wrong.
  • Review whether the intervention changes the pattern.

sessions.title: Key Messages to Take Back to the Classroom
sessions.content:
Key Messages to Take Back to the Classroom

The core professional stance.

  • Not every difficult behaviour is a stress response.
  • Not every stressed child will look distressed.
  • Regulation comes before complex reasoning during high arousal.
  • Connection and boundaries are complementary, not competing approaches.
  • Effective behaviour support teaches what to do instead.
  • Persistent or serious concerns require collaboration, documentation and appropriate referral.

sessions.title: The Goal Is Not Perfect Behaviour
sessions.content:
The Goal Is Not Perfect Behaviour.

The goal is to create classrooms where children are safe enough to learn, supported enough to regulate, and taught enough to succeed.

Thank you.
